). Specifically, while positive valence seems to have little effect, negative valence appears to significantly increase the amount of details that are remembered. For example,
Kensinger et al. (2007)
have shown that participants are more accurate in remembering visual details of negative valanced items (e.g., “a green and black snake with yellow eyes”) compared to positive items (e.g., “a cake”). Obviously, there could be visual confounds that might lead to more detailed memory for negative compared to positive stimuli. It has been shown, however, that even if visual confounds are controlled for, the effect of valence on memory accuracy prevails. One prominent example is the study by
Kensinger and Schacter (2006)
, which measured the amount of details Red Sox fans and Yankee fans could report from a baseball game and found that supporters of the losing team had more detailed memories. In this instance, the visual information was matched between the groups, but what differed was the either positive or negative appraisal of the event that led to differences in memory accuracy.
decision.reason: The paper frames its goal as conceptually replicating the collective finding across 'several experiments by Kensinger and colleagues' ('findings by Kensinger and colleagues (c.f. Kensinger, 2009a, b)'). The shipped citation (Kensinger, 2009a, Emotion Review) is a single-author review article cited jointly with the commentary reply Kensinger (2009b) via 'c.f.', and under Step 2 of the codebook review articles must be ruled out in favor of primary studies. In the Introduction, the author cites multiple primary empirical papers by Kensinger and colleagues as examples—including two behavioral detail-memory studies (Kensinger et al., 2007; Kensinger and Schacter, 2006) as well as neuroimaging studies (Kensinger and Schacter, 2008; Mickley and Kensinger, 2008)—without specifying a single replacement primary paper for row 731. Because the two behavioral primary targets fit equally well and no unique primary study identity can be established for row 731, original is undeterminable.

Addressing the dependency objection: under Step 3 of the codebook, replication outcomes are coded per empirical original study, and a set-wide verdict applies only when all candidate originals belong to a tested set. Here, the shipped row identifies a non-empirical review paper (Kensinger, 2009a), which cannot itself carry an empirical replication outcome, while the replacement primary study for row 731 remains unresolved (undeterminable). Furthermore, the candidate primary citations in the Introduction are not homogeneous: while the author confirms the collective behavioral detail-memory hypothesis ('confirmed Kensinger’s hypothesis'; 'provided support for Kensinger’s (2009a, b) hypothesis that, independent of arousal, negative affect facilitates the encoding of sensory details')—which would conditionally support 'successful' if row 731 were mapped specifically to the behavioral primary studies (Kensinger et al., 2007 or Kensinger and Schacter, 2006)—the candidate Kensinger references also include neuroimaging studies (Kensinger and Schacter, 2008; Mickley and Kensinger, 2008) whose neural-activation findings were not retested ('Future neuroimaging studies could investigate the effect of emotional valence on memory encoding of highly similar stimulus material to provide corroborative neural evidence'). Without a resolved primary original mapping for row 731, an unconditional 'successful' outcome cannot be assigned, making outcome undeterminable.
